home.heroSubtitle: India Eurasia Research Forum (IERF) is an independent initiative dedicated to promoting research, dialogue and people to people cooperation between India and Eurasia.
home.visionBody: The India-Eurasia corridor represents one of the most consequential geopolitical axes of the 21st century. IERF's research examines trade flows exceeding  billion annually, the strategic implications of the International North-South Transport Corridor (INSTC), and India's evolving partnerships with Central Asian republics. In a rapidly transforming Eurasia, marked by multi-vector foreign policies and connectivity realignments, IERF serves as a vital enabler for strategic re-engagement.
home.visionQuote: "Driving evidence-based continental re-engagement to help India build enduring strategic depth."

about.subtitle: Bridging the intellectual and strategic gap between India and Eurasia.
about.whoWeAre: The India Eurasia Research Forum (IERF) is India’s first research network dedicated to a comprehensive study of the Eurasian region. Our team comprises early career researchers, journalists, policymakers and emerging voices from India’s leading public universities, including the Jawaharlal Nehru University and the University of Delhi. Together, we endeavour to bridge the intellectual and strategic gap between India and Eurasia, a region comprising Russia, Greater Central Asia and the Caucasus. To bridge this gap, IERF operates at the intersection of scholarly rigour and diplomatic engagement. The forum will serve as a platform for advancing cooperation and trust across Eurasia while supporting India’s evolving global engagement by fostering cross-border cultural exchanges through an interdisciplinary approach.
about.whatWeDoIntro: IERF aims to foster informed dialogue and multidimensional engagement between India and Eurasia. Currently, as part of our foundational mission, IERF’s work is based on four pillars:

pillars.title: Research
pillars.description: Conduct in-depth research on Eurasian geopolitics, economics, and culture to build research pathways between India and Eurasia. Promote and build a comprehensive repository of Indian perspectives on Eurasia.

pillars.title: Dialogue
pillars.description: Facilitate informed dialogue through publications, seminars, and conferences. Foster greater cultural understanding and civilisational dialogue between India and the Eurasian countries through the Volga to Ganga Dialogue series.

pillars.title: Engagement
pillars.description: Promote multidimensional engagement across India and Eurasia through academic collaboration and public diplomacy initiatives. To promote Track 2 dialogues between India and the Eurasian countries in the future.

pillars.title: Policy Impact
pillars.description: Provide up-to-date & policy-relevant insights to decision-makers and industry leaders. To shape the policy landscape of foreign policy-making in the region on Eurasian affairs, particularly in regional cooperation, resource geopolitics, economic developments, and civilisational discourse.

visionParagraphs: At the India Eurasia Research Forum (IERF), we believe that informed research and open dialogue are essential to building resilient partnerships and sustained engagement. The forum provides a platform for researchers, policymakers, and practitioners from India and Eurasia to explore the deep historical, cultural, and strategic ties that connect these dynamic regions, ensuring that academic enquiry and research effectively inform public discourse and shape the policy landscape.

As part of IERF’s vision, we promote a homegrown Indian perspective on Eurasian affairs. Our long-term vision is to become a leading India-origin academic platform that promotes research and publications on all aspects of Eurasian political, economic, and socio-cultural developments, particularly those that can have implications for India.

IERF’s vision also extends to bringing India and Eurasia closer together — not just through analysis, publications and talks, but through shared stories and ideas that bridge gaps. We believe Eurasian studies need to be reimagined in Indian academic and policy-making circles, and IERF intends to fill this space.

Regional Security in the Eurasian context

Eurasian civilisations and cultural hybridity in the twenty-first century
whyIerfParagraphs: India’s role on the global stage is expanding rapidly, with a growing think-tank culture, particularly those dedicated to studying the various dimensions of India’s global engagements. While India’s global footprint grows, dedicated research on the vast Eurasian landmass — a region closely intertwined with India’s history and vital to its future — has often been overlooked.

At IERF, we recognise the need to overcome this inertia by building an effective research ecosystem that provides up-to-date analysis of the latest developments, policy-relevant insights and fosters cross-border knowledge exchanges between India and Eurasia. IERF remains open to engaging with people from walks of life interested in exploring the new frontiers of Eurasian studies. We follow an inclusive working style and adhere to the highest standards of academic enquiry.

leadership.name: Rahul Gupta
leadership.bio: Rahul Gupta is a Senior Research Fellow with the Centre for Russian and Central Asian Studies at the School of International Studies, Jawaharlal Nehru University, New Delhi, India. He is currently pursuing a PhD at the same institution. His research interests include Eurasian geopolitics, regional connectivity between South and Central Asia, and international organisations in the Global South, with a focus on BRICS and SCO. An early career researcher specialising in post-Soviet studies, he has published extensively, including with SAGE, Routledge and the London School of Economics and Political Science Review of Books.

leadership.name: Sujal Yadav
leadership.bio: Sujal Yadav is a Senior Research Fellow with the Centre for Russian and Central Asian Studies at the School of International Studies, Jawaharlal Nehru University, New Delhi, India. He is currently pursuing a PhD at the same institution. His research interests include Russian foreign policy, cultural diplomacy, Russian literature, and cultural studies. An early career researcher specialising in contemporary Russian studies, her primary focus is on how non-traditional actors/institutions interact with traditional actors to shape global affairs.

technicalTeam.name: Abhishek Singh
technicalTeam.bio: Abhishek leads the technical vision at IERF. With a Master's in Technology from Jawaharlal Nehru University, he brings deep expertise in full-stack web architecture, AI/ML systems integration, and modern DevOps practices. He has architected platforms serving institutions, e-commerce businesses, and international research organizations.

technicalTeam.name: Avadhesh Kumar
technicalTeam.bio: Avadhesh Kumar is a researcher at IIT Delhi and co-founder of an AI startup. Currently pursuing an M.Tech in Computer Technology, his work focuses on the intersection of systems engineering and advanced artificial intelligence, with specific expertise in high-performance Transformer models and mathematical reasoning in LLMs. He leads the technical development and systems architecture for IERF.

advisor.name: Dr. Pravesh Kumar Gupta
advisor.bio:
Dr Pravesh Kumar Gupta is an Associate Fellow at the Vivekananda International Foundation (VIF) and an expert on Eurasian geopolitics. He holds a PhD in Central Asian Studies from the School of International Studies, Jawaharlal Nehru University (JNU), New Delhi. His research focuses on the society and politics of the Central Asian Republics, the geopolitics of Central and South Asia, energy security, and trans-regional connectivity and energy linkages between Central and South Asia.

Dr Gupta's views are regularly published in leading platforms, such as The Hindustan Times, The Financial Express, Dunyo Information Agency (Information Agency of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Uzbekistan), and the Valdai Discussion Club. He has authored a book and contributed chapters to several edited volumes in his areas of specialisation. He has also served as an International Election Observer during the Presidential Elections in Uzbekistan in 2021 and the constitutional referendum in 2023.

scholarlyNetwork.name: Kishan Srinivas
scholarlyNetwork.bio: Kishan Srinivas is a Master's student of Political Science at the Department of Political Science, University of Delhi, India. He holds a B.Tech in Electronics and Communication Engineering from Presidency University, Bangalore, India. With an interdisciplinary academic background, Kishan's areas of research interest include the intersection of Science and Technology with Political Science and International Relations. His research also includes studying the role of technology in Diplomacy and International Relations. He has previously worked as an AI and Geopolitical Risk intern at Hozint.

scholarlyNetwork.name: Arkadyute Nath
scholarlyNetwork.bio: Arkadyute has completed his undergraduate studies in English literature from Hansraj College, University of Delhi. He is currently working as a Program Assistant and Social Media Manager at TGMC, under ArtSpeaks India.

scholarlyNetwork.name: Ravi Raj
scholarlyNetwork.bio: Ravi Raj is a research scholar at the Centre for Russian and Central Asian Studies, School of International Studies, Jawaharlal Nehru University (JNU), New Delhi. His research focuses on nuclear nonproliferation, peacebuilding and conflict resolution in Eurasia, energy geopolitics, and India–Russia relations. He has participated in several international academic and policy forums, including the Nasser Fellowship in Egypt. He regularly contributes analytical pieces on global and regional security affairs.

scholarlyNetwork.name: Vaibhavi Gupta
scholarlyNetwork.bio: Vaibhavi Gupta is a Junior Research Fellow with the Centre for Russian and Central Asian Studies, School of International Studies, Jawaharlal Nehru University, New Delhi, India. She is currently pursuing a PhD at the same institution. Her research interests include post-colonial and critical theories of IR, Russian literature and philosophy. As an early career researcher specialising in post-Soviet and contemporary Russian studies, her primary focus is on how non-traditional actors/institutions interact with traditional actors to shape global affairs.

scholarlyNetwork.name: Saumya Tomar
scholarlyNetwork.bio: Saumya Tomar is a Junior Research Fellow at the Centre for Russian and Central Asian Studies, School of International Studies, Jawaharlal Nehru University, New Delhi. She is a PhD candidate at the same institution. Her research interests include climate change, environmental security and environmental governance in Eurasia, with a special focus on the Arctic and Baltic Region. Her work examines how environmental transformation influences governance structures, disrupts economic activity, and shapes geopolitical dynamics in the Post-Soviet space.

scholarlyNetwork.name: Aditya Harsh
scholarlyNetwork.bio: Aditya is a PhD candidate at the Centre for Russian and Central Asian Studies (CRCAS), School of International Studies, Jawaharlal Nehru University (JNU). His research engages with foreign policy analysis, especially Russia's foreign policy behaviour and India's strategic positioning within Russian policy frameworks. He has written on issues such as soft power, shifting geopolitical alignments, and the evolving dynamics of regional and global politics. His research aims to provide policy-relevant insights into contemporary geopolitical trends and their implications for India's foreign policy and regional security.

scholarlyNetwork.name: Avik Sarkar
scholarlyNetwork.bio: Avik Sarkar is a Senior Research Fellow with the Centre for Political Studies, Jawaharlal Nehru University, New Delhi. He works at the intersection of agrarian political economy and Subaltern Studies in India. His PhD thesis interrogates the fall of the world's longest-serving democratically elected Communist government in the Indian state of West Bengal. He is also interested in colonial-era Indian engagements with Germany and Russia. With deep interest in political philosophy, he advocates the need to blend Indian and non-Eurocentric conceptual universes.

scholarlyNetwork.name: Harshal Raj Patel
scholarlyNetwork.bio: Harshal Raj Patel completed his undergraduate studies in Philosophy at Hansraj College, University of Delhi. His final-year dissertation examined meritocracy and the concept of justice. His research interests include society, diplomatic history, and South Asian affairs. Alongside his academic pursuits, he has worked as a consultant at a New Delhi-based political consultancy. He is also a freelance columnist and contributes regularly to The Tribune, covering nationalism, geopolitics, and diplomatic history.

publications.title: The Eurasian Digital Silk Road: Can India and Eurasia Rewire the Future of Work and Knowledge?
publications.author: Yash Singh Sisodiya
publications.description: A quiet transformation is underway as a 'Digital Silk Route' takes shape across Eurasia, potentially reshaping how societies collaborate and work together beyond physical highways and pipelines.
publications.content:
The Eurasian Digital Silk Road: Can India and Eurasia Rewire the Future of Work and Knowledge?

Over the last decade, discussions on India’s engagement with Eurasia have been marked by themes including geopolitics, energy cooperation, and strategic connectivity initiatives. The transport corridors connecting India to Central Asia and Russia, such as the International North-South Transport Corridor (INSTC), have lacked momentum compared with other Eurasian connectivity projects, such as the Middle Corridor and the Belt and Road Initiative, which have attracted greater global policy attention in recent years.

However, a quieter transformation is underway as a “Digital Silk Route” takes shape across Eurasia. There is a possibility that, in the absence of physical connectivity, India and Eurasia take a digital route that goes beyond highways, pipelines, and railways, reshaping how societies collaborate, exchange knowledge, and work together in the global labour force.

This transformation will not merely be technological but will also entail a deeper restructuring of economic opportunities, digital governance, and knowledge networks linking India with Eurasia, extending across the wider Eurasian region. As the digital infrastructure expands across the region, Eurasia and India can continue to strengthen their digital public platforms, and the region can witness the formation of new corridors- not made of steel or concrete, but of data flows, digital platforms, and virtual collaboration.

From Physical Connectivity to Digital Corridors

For decades, India has faced structural constraints in engaging with Eurasia, particularly geographic barriers that limit physical connectivity. The region’s connectivity landscape has historically been shaped by complex political and logistical realities that make trade routes both expensive and time-consuming. India’s connectivity with the region has been disrupted since the partition of South Asia in 1947, and the situation has remained similar since then. However, digital connectivity and infrastructure corridors are now helping to bypass this geographical hurdle.

Today, country-level cooperation between India and the Eurasian region includes technology partnerships, digital infrastructure development, and innovations. Digital connectivity initiatives—sometimes described as elements of a “Digital Silk Road”—are helping countries collaborate across fields such as fintech, cybersecurity, artificial intelligence, and digital governance. These new forms of cooperation are gradually complementing the traditional connectivity initiatives between India and Central Asia.

For India, which has successfully developed one of the world’s most extensive Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI) ecosystems and platforms such as Aadhaar and UPI, this represents an opportunity for a new form of technological cooperation with the emerging digital economies of Eurasia. whereas, in the context of the Eurasian states, they also gain new partners to diversify their current technology partnerships and improve their digital capabilities. Thus, representing a new form of mutual interest for Eurasian connectivity.

The Rise of Transnational Digital Workspaces

The most significant impact of this emerging digital corridor is its influence on the future of work. Across Eurasia, young professionals are increasingly participating in remote employment and digital freelancing. India’s large pool of technology professionals and its increasing start-up ecosystem are already deeply integrated into global digital labour markets. As connectivity across Eurasia improves, these networks are expanding to include new partners in Central Asian and Eastern European economies.

Besides the digital workspaces, digital collaboration is also redefining the educational and knowledge exchanges. Universities, technology institutes, and research centres across India and Eurasia are expanding. Online learning platforms, virtual academic collaborations, and digital research partnerships are facilitating intellectual inclusion. Such initiatives have received more focus since the COVID-19 pandemic, which accelerated the adoption of remote communication technologies.

In practical terms, this means that an Indian software developer in Bengaluru, a start-up founder in Tashkent, and a data scientist in Moscow can collaborate in real time without geographical constraints. These digital interactions are slowly creating a transnational ecosystem of knowledge production and innovation, which was once dependent solely on diplomatic and economic ties.

Digital Connectivity and Youth Mobility

One of the significant byproducts of the Digital Silk Route is Youth mobility and skill exchange. India’s demographic profile, characterised by a technologically skilled youth, positions the country as an important contributor to Eurasia’s emerging digital economy. On the contrary, numerous Eurasian countries are investing in digital transformation strategies that require skilled workers and collaborative innovation networks.

India’s growing partnerships with Central Asian countries in areas such as education, information technology, and digital governance illustrate how these relationships are evolving beyond traditional strategic engagement and gradually expanding the scope of India–Eurasia relations from state-centric diplomacy to society-driven digital exchange. Students, entrepreneurs, and technology professionals increasingly serve as informal ambassadors of this emerging digital partnership. Through hackathons, academic partnerships, start-up accelerators, and technology conferences, new collaborative communities are forming across the region. These interactions contribute not only to economic cooperation but also to long-term cultural and intellectual linkages.

Strategic and Governance Challenges

Despite its promise, the Digital Silk Route also presents complex governance challenges. Questions surrounding data security, digital sovereignty, regulatory standards, and cybersecurity remain central to discussions about digital cooperation across Eurasia. Countries maintain different approaches to digital governance, and aligning these frameworks will require frequently organised policy dialogues.

Furthermore, as urban centres rapidly integrate into digital economies, rural and tribal regions in India often lag behind. Addressing this digital divide will be essential if the benefits of digital connectivity are to be distributed more equitably across societies. Both India and Eurasian countries are facing this issue at the onset of digitisation.

From a strategic perspective, the digital connectivity intersects with broader geopolitical competition over technology ecosystems and data standards. As global powers increasingly view digital infrastructure as a strategic domain, countries across Eurasia are navigating complex technological partnerships. India’s approach, often characterised by openness, technological pluralism, and its successful experience with scalable digital public platforms, could offer an alternative model for collaborative digital development to both regions.

A New Phase in India–Eurasia Relations

This development in the evolution of the Digital Silk Route can take India-Eurasia relations into a new chapter, defined not only by agreements and projects but also by connections in knowledge, innovation, and digital labour forces. Though not readily apparent, these connections may eventually prove more transformative than those along highways or pipelines. In the long term, digital connectivity may change the very idea of regional cooperation in Eurasia. Instead of understanding regional connectivity only in terms of physical routes, policymakers may come to appreciate the value of data flows, digital entrepreneurship, and collaborative innovation in regional cooperation.

For India, engaging with Eurasia’s digital transformation offers an opportunity to forge deeper alliances that transcend traditional security considerations. For Eurasian states, collaboration with India’s vast digital ecosystem can provide access to a one-billion-plus market, technological expertise, innovation networks, and a dynamic knowledge economy to systematically scale digital infrastructure to the last mile.

The Digital Silk Route might still be in its formative stages, but it is an example of how connectivity in the twenty-first century is driven less by geography than by people, platforms, and ideas. As connectivity continues to evolve, it could prove to be one of the most significant underpinnings of future India-Eurasia engagement.
publications.authorBio: Yash Singh Sisodiya is a social sciences researcher based in Indore and is currently affiliated with Twisting Memoirs Publication as a Research Publication Manager. His work focuses on social policy, governance, gender studies, and development research in India. He has published extensively in national and international journals and has previously been affiliated with institutions including Devi Ahilya University, UNICEF, ICSSR, and LBSNAA.

publications.title: Intercultural Dialogue in Practice: Lessons from Russian-African Delegation Work
publications.author: Ekaterina Pimenova
publications.description: An insightful exploration of interculturality and cultural diplomacy in international relations, drawing on firsthand experiences with African delegations in Russia.
publications.content:
To start with, Mikhail Bakhtin, the renowned Russian philosopher and literary scholar, wrote in his work "The Aesthetics of Verbal Creation" (1986): "There exists a very persistent, but one-sided and therefore incorrect, understanding that to better understand a foreign culture, one must, as it were, migrate into it and, forgetting one's own, look at the world through the eyes of that foreign culture". The idea of a real conversation between cultures has remained central to current discussions of cultural interaction.

It resonates deeply with the French concept of 'interculturalité’(interculturality) – it is not about the assimilation or dilution of cultural differences, but about their recognition and respectful engagement. This understanding of intercultural dialogue goes well with the work of contemporary French philosopher and sinologist François Jullien. He does not compare cultures but seeks to enrich one through the other by exploring the 'distance' (écart) between Chinese and European thought. The philosopher reveals their unspoken assumptions and opens a space for good encounter — an approach that aligns with the principle of interculturality.

As an independent cultural diplomat and interpreter-attachée, I engage with the notion of interculturality in my professional environment: international forums, conferences, and world events. There is a common cliché that interpreters translate worlds, but in reality, they work with cultural codes and national traditions. By sharing my experience of work with different African delegations, I want to show how these cultural codes are put into practice and why they matter for building trust. The principles of intercultural dialogue are universal and can be applied not only to Russian–African relations but also to any encounter between distant cultures — including the growing partnership between India and the vast Eurasian space.

1. The Mooré Word That Changed Everything: Respect speaks louder than fluency.

I had been working with the Burkinabé delegation for days — formal, correct, professional environment. Then one morning, I greeted the head delegate in Mooré, his native language. Just a few words: "Good morning, I hope you rested well." His face suddenly transformed. He laughed, corrected my pronunciation with delight, and introduced me to his colleagues as "the most Burkinabé of all the Russians". The formal wall between us crumbled instantly.

So it is sometimes not crucial to master a language to master trust. The mere attempt — the willingness to step into someone's linguistic world — signals respect. And respect is the currency of mutual dialogue.

2. When Bronze Spoke Louder Than Words: Culture builds bridges that politics can not build.

At the "Grandeur in Bronze" exhibition in Novosibirsk, I wasn't just translating words; I was in two worlds at once. Russian visitors gazed at traditional Burkinabé sculptures with full of questions: "What does this figure mean? Why this posture? Who made it?" The delegates didn't just answer; however, they came alive, sharing stories of their ancestors, their myths, and their identity. And the Russians listened, truly listened!

A photo from the Bronze exhibition in Novosibirsk, Russian Federation

To sum up, the art really speaks directly to the heart. When people connect through culture, they stop being "delegates" and "foreigners" — they become human beings sharing something precious. That’s why cultural diplomacy is about the exchange of human experiences, not competition.

3. The Karavai That Welcomed a Delegation: The immediate emotional connection.

I will never forget the arrival of a delegation at the airport. It was their first visit to Russia, and they were tired after a long flight. But when they stepped into the arrival hall, they were met with a traditional Russian welcome: a round loaf of bread (karavai) with a small cup of salt. According to Russian custom, this is how guests are honoured and welcomed.

Their faces changed instantly. Surprise turned into smiles, and the formal tension dissolved. Soon, everyone was taking photos, asking questions about this tradition, and sharing stories of similar customs in their own culture.

That small ritual did what hours of official negotiations could not: it truly opened hearts. The bread and salt spoke a language that needed no translation. It is the language of hospitality and respect. From that moment, the entire forum felt different. The delegation was not just a group of officials; they were guests who had been truly welcomed.

This experience taught me that interculturality lives in these gestures — in the willingness to share your culture’s soul with someone from another world. A simple loaf of bread can become a bridge, reminding us that beneath all our differences. We all value kindness and respect.

These experiences have taught me that interculturality is not a theoretical concept reserved for academic journals. It is a living practice, existing in the smallest moments of human lives. What makes dialogue mutual is not the absence of difference, but the courage to acknowledge it. Mikhail Bakhtin was right: we do not need to abandon our own culture to understand another. Instead, we need to find the space between — the place where two worlds can meet, each bringing its own light to illuminate what the other might otherwise miss. This is precisely what François Jullien calls the écart: not a gap to be bridged, but a creative distance that allows each culture to see itself more clearly through the eyes of the other.

In my work as an interpreter-attachée, I have learned that the most powerful tools of diplomacy are not technical skill or linguistic precision: they are curiosity, respect and humility. These lessons, I reckon, are universal. Whether the encounter is between Russia and Africa, India and Central Asia, or any other combination of cultures, the principles remain the same. The partnership between India and the Eurasian space, rich with history and potential, will thrive not only on economic agreements and political alliances but on the countless small moments of genuine human connection that build trust over time.

Interculturality is not about erasing differences. It is about celebrating them. It is not about finding common ground by flattening what makes us unique, but about creating a space where our differences can coexist, enrich each other, and open new possibilities for understanding. And that, perhaps, is the most important lesson of all: the future of international relations lies not in protocols and agreements, but in the simple, courageous act of meeting one another as human beings.
publications.authorBio: Ekaterina Pimenova has been working as an independent cultural diplomat and attachée for 3 years now. Although her experience primarily revolves around working with African delegations, Ms Pimenova believes that her experience can be applied to the development of cultural diplomacy between India and Eurasia.

publications.title: From Ayni to Chabahar: India’s Strategic Retreat from Central Asia?
publications.author: Rahul Gupta
publications.description: While India’s exit from the Ayni Airbase was seen as a symbolic loss, the winding down of operations at Chabahar could significantly undermine India’s Central Asia outreach and weaken its long-term presence in Eurasia.
publications.imageFootnote: A view of the Shahid Beheshti terminal at Chabahar Port, Iran
publications.content:
For the last two decades, India tried to expand its presence in its extended neighbourhood, a set of regions beyond South Asia which significantly affect its growth and security. While the extended neighbourhood approach towards West Asia and East Asia was relatively successful, registering significant growth in terms of trade and investments in the last decade, Central Asia continues to lie on the outskirts of India’s Extended Neighbourhood despite tall claims. The latest developments in the region, such as India’s exit from the Ayni Airbase in Tajikistan last year, and more significantly, its decision to pull out of the Chabahar port project following the expiring US sanctions' exemption will diminish India’s presence in Central Asia. The ongoing US-Israeli attack on Iran and rising Chinese and Pakistani footprint in the region might further signal India’s strategic retreat from a geopolitically significant Eurasia.

Central Asia’s significance in India’s Extended Neighbourhood

For much of the post-Soviet period, Indian policy makers and analysts acknowledged India’s strategic interests in Central Asia, emphasising its immense hydrocarbon and critical mineral reserves. The region’s significance was further supported by South Asia’s historical linkages with Central Asia, as for several centuries, the Silk Road was the conduit of Eurasian continental trade and the site of hybridisation of cultures across Eurasia. From a regional security perspective, India’s security was closely tied to the region as its threat perceptions and many of its ruling dynasties originated from Central Asia. Meanwhile, India realised it had limited options and instruments to project influence in the region despite its importance in Eurasian geopolitics.

Following the dissolution of the Soviet Union, India recognised the newly independent Central Asian republics, terming the region “high priority”. However, domestic economic restructuring in India and post-Soviet economic headwinds and political instability in Central Asia kept bilateral trade below the potential. Despite inconsequential trade turnover as part of each other’s total foreign trade, India continued to reiterate Central Asia’s significance in the extended neighbourhood. Focusing on high-level diplomatic outreach to the region, Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s visited all the five Central Asian republics in 2015, a first in India’s diplomatic history. Regional security was another area of concern for India as the spread of religious fundamentalism and extremism from the Afghanistan-Pakistan region made it necessary to have a security presence in Central Asia.

India’s connectivity push in Central Asia in the Post-Cold War era

Riding on the geopolitical momentum of the twenty-first century and in response to emerging energy and human security challenges, India shifted it geoeconomic approach to the region. It signed the multi-modal International North South Transport Corridor in 2000 with Russia and Iran to develop overland trade between India, Iran and Russia, with the objective to reach markets in Central Asia and Europe. Following years of negotiations over funding, customs regulations, and other operational bottlenecks, India soon realised the importance of Iran in connecting with Central Asia and Afghanistan. The INSTC’s transnational scale and huge investment demands, however, nudged India to develop more regionally-oriented, Iran-linked infrastructure to connect with Central Asia.

Chabahar and the illusion of regional connectivity

In 2015, India signed the Chabahar port project with Iran, projecting it as a gateway to Central Asia and to deliver humanitarian aid to Afghanistan. Iran’s only deep-water sea port, Chabahar addressed Indian concerns over Pakistan’s denial of overland access to Afghanistan. The port’s regional profile rose when India signed the Ashgabat Agreement in 2018, and in 2021, proposed Chabahar’s integration in INSTC, projecting Indian influence in the region for the first time. India endorsed the port’s regional utility by successfully lobbying the US government to exempt Chabahar from sanctions. In May 2024, India’s Indian Ports Global Limited (IPGL) signed a ten-year contract with Iran’s Port and Maritime Organisation (PMO) to develop the Shahid-Beheshti terminal of Chabahar port, committing $120 million for developing the port and offering a $250 million line of credit for expanding Chabahar-related regional infrastructure.

India’s ad hoc approach to Central Asia

Evidentially, Chabahar became the lodestar of India’s connectivity push with Central Asia in the last decade. It was also projected as India’s only viable land-link with Afghanistan, delivering over 2.5 million tons of wheat and humanitarian aid during the Covid-19 pandemic to the embattled country. India’s bilateral trade with Central Asian republics also doubled in the last decade, partly due to Chabahar’s operationalalisation and due to strengthening of the institutional framework of relations through dialogue and summit-level frameworks in 2019 and 2022. Modest growth in India-Central Asia trade notwithstanding, the quantum of trade still remains much less than that of Russia, China and Turkey’s trade with the region. Nevertheless, India’s excellent relations with Iran and Central Asia made Chabahar a successful example of India’s regional diplomacy in an otherwise complex region, giving landlocked Central Asian countries access to the Indian Ocean.

US sanctions on Iran and India’s Strategic Retreat from Central Asia

India’s optimism over its foreign policy posturing of strategic autonomy, however, turned to be short lived in the wake of the US President’s twenty-five percent tariffs threat to countries doing trade with Iran early this year. Facing rising US pressure, India had already been reducing oil and gas imports from Iran, with bilateral trade going down from $17 billion in 2018-2019 to $1.68 billion in 2024-2025, but the latest US threat comes as a significant setback. The Economic Times reported early this year that following US’ sanctions exemption expiring in September last year, India had begun winding up operations at Chabahar, transferring the remaining financial commitment to Iran and exiting from operations at the port.

This news comes at the backdrop of another revelation in October last year that India had exited the Ayni Airbase, a small functional airbase on the outskirt of the Tajik capital of Dushanbe, which India refurbished in the early 2000s and used as a listening post near the Tajik-Afghan border. The exit from Ayni Airbase last year was still seen as a symbolic loss. However, the winding up of Indian operations at Chabahar, a project in which India has invested close to half a billion dollars and extensive diplomatic capital, will have lasting repercussions.

On a bilateral level, India’s already strained trade ties with Iran comes in the backdrop of the rapidly evolving situation in West Asia. As the US-Israeli attack on Iran unfolds, reports suggest aerial damage around the port city of Chabahar, even though there is no damage reported at the India operated Shahid Beheshti terminal. However, the Israeli-US strikes on Iran’s critical infrastructure will complicate India’s limited operational role in the port, and discourage private investment in the future. In a region which India considers its extended neighbourhood, stepping down from Chabahar without an alternative will undermine India’s already limited engagement with Central Asia. On the other hand, it will strengthen Pakistan’s credibility to the Central Asian republics for accessing the Indian ocean through Chinese-led BRI infrastructure. In the wider region, ceding space to China and Pakistan will erode India’s long-term presence in Eurasia.
publications.authorBio: Rahul Gupta is a Senior Research Fellow with the Centre for Russian and Central Asian Studies at the School of International Studies, Jawaharlal Nehru University, New Delhi, India. He is currently pursuing a PhD at the same institution. His research interests include Eurasian geopolitics, regional connectivity between South and Central Asia, and international organisations in the Global South, with a focus on BRICS and SCO. An early career researcher specialising in post-Soviet studies, he has published extensively, including with SAGE, Routledge and the London School of Economics and Political Science Review of Books. He is also the Founder Director of India Eurasia Research Forum (IERF).

publications.title: A Journey of Dialogue and Discovery: My Experience in India
publications.author: Nurbolat Toktamys
publications.description: In 2025, I had the privilege of visiting India as a delegate of the 3rd India Central Asia Youth Delegation Forum. For me, the journey was more than a diplomatic event or an international conference.
publications.content:
In 2025, I had the privilege of visiting India as a delegate of the 3rd India Central Asia Youth Delegation Forum. For me, the journey was more than a diplomatic event or an international conference. It was a deeply meaningful opportunity to experience a country that has long maintained historical, cultural, and intellectual ties with Central Asia.

As someone who grew up in Kazakhstan and now teaches chemistry at the Nazarbayev Intellectual School in Turkestan, I have always been interested in how countries collaborate through education, science, and youth engagement. The forum offered exactly that: a platform where young professionals from Central Asia could exchange ideas with Indian counterparts about regional cooperation, innovation, and cultural understanding.

From the moment I arrived, India left a strong impression on me. The scale, diversity, and energy of the country was remarkable. Cities moved at an intense rhythm, yet there was also a sense of openness and curiosity among the people I met. India felt both ancient and modern at the same time – a place where centuries-old traditions coexist with technological innovation and ambitious economic development.

A traditional Indian reception for the Central Asian Youth Delegation, March, 2025

The Youth Forum itself was organised at a very high level by New Delhi. The program included discussions with policymakers, scholars, and young leaders who shared perspectives on regional cooperation between India and Central Asia. These conversations highlighted the strategic importance of strengthening people-to-people connections and building cross-cultural connections. While governments can establish diplomatic frameworks, it is often students, researchers, and young professionals who build the real bridges between societies.

One of the most memorable aspects of the visit was interacting with fellow participants from different countries. Delegates from Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Uzbekistan, and Turkmenistan had the opportunity to share their views on regional development and cultural exchange. At the same time, Indian participants introduced us to the intellectual and cultural diversity of their country. These conversations were not limited to formal sessions. Some of the most valuable exchanges happened during informal discussions, shared meals, and cultural visits.

India’s cultural richness also left a lasting impression on me. Walking through historical landmarks and observing daily life offered insights that no book or lecture could fully convey. The architecture, art, and traditions reflected a long and complex history that has shaped the identity of the country. At the same time, I was struck by how strongly young Indians are engaging with global issues such as technology, entrepreneurship, and sustainable development.

Another aspect that impressed me was India’s commitment to education and knowledge exchange. As an educator myself, I was particularly interested in how universities, research institutions, and policy think tanks collaborate to support innovation and international dialogue. The forum demonstrated that India sees education and youth engagement as important tools of public diplomacy and regional cooperation.

At the Indian Institute of Technology, Delhi, India

For me, the visit also reinforced the historical connections between Central Asia and India, which are more than a millennium old. For centuries, trade routes, cultural exchange, and intellectual interaction linked the two regions. Today, these connections continue in new forms through academic partnerships, cultural initiatives, and youth forums such as the one I attended. It was inspiring to see how modern diplomacy is built upon these historical ties.

One of my main takeaways from the experience is the importance of dialogue and mutual understanding. When people from different countries meet and share their perspectives, stereotypes disappear, and genuine partnerships can emerge. International cooperation becomes more meaningful when it is supported by personal relationships and cultural awareness.

As a teacher, this experience also influenced how I think about education. I realised that preparing students for the future requires more than strong academic knowledge. It also requires global awareness, cultural openness, and the ability to collaborate with people from different backgrounds. Experiences like the India – Central Asia Youth Forum demonstrate the value of international engagement in shaping the next generation of leaders.

From a meeting with educationists and industry leaders

When I returned to Kazakhstan, I shared my experiences with colleagues and students. Many of them were curious to learn more about India – its culture, society, and opportunities for collaboration. This exchange of stories and perspectives is exactly how international understanding grows: through individual experiences that inspire broader curiosity and dialogue.

Looking back, my visit to India was not only a professional opportunity but also a personal journey of discovery. It allowed me to see a country that is vibrant, diverse, and forward-looking. More importantly, it reminded me that meaningful cooperation between regions begins with human connections.

Initiatives such as the India – Central Asia Youth Forum play an important role in strengthening these connections. By bringing together young people from different societies, they help build the foundations for long-term cooperation and goodwill.

I hope that exchanges between India and Central Asia will continue to grow in the coming years. The potential for collaboration in education, science, culture, and innovation is enormous. For young professionals like me, participating in such initiatives is both a privilege and a responsibility – to carry forward the spirit of dialogue and partnership that these forums represents.
publications.authorBio: Nurbolat Toktamys teaches chemistry at the Nazarbayev Intellectual School of Science and Mathematics in Turkestan, Kazakhstan. He mentors students in scientific research and actively promotes international youth dialogue, educational collaboration, and cultural exchange between Central Asia and the broader Eurasian region.

publications.title: Eurasia in India's Strategic Calculus
publications.author: Dr. Pravesh Kumar Gupta
publications.description: IERF serves as a vital enabler in a rapidly transforming Eurasia, driving evidence-based continental re-engagement to help India build enduring strategic depth.
publications.imageFootnote: A view of the Rashtrapati Bhawan, New Delhi, India
publications.content:
A view of the Rashtrapati Bhawan, New Delhi, India

Globally, Eurasia refers to the world's largest continuous landmass, combining Europe and Asia as a single supercontinent. The term originated in the 19th century as a geographical construct. Later, it was popularised by political geographers to describe the combined Europe-Asia landmass without artificial divisions like the Ural Mountains. In geopolitical discourse, it gained prominence through Halford Mackinder's Heartland theory in the early 20th century. Mackinder’s Heartland theory suggested that control of the Eurasian core (especially Central Asia) is pivotal to global dominance. In the post-Soviet era, this geopolitical reading of Eurasia has evolved. Russian thinkers like Alexander Dugin advocated it as Eurasianism and have framed it as a unique civilizational space blending Slavic, Turkic, and steppe elements.

Because of the geostrategic location and abundance of natural resources, Eurasia has long been a playground for major power play in the twenty-first century. For each major power engaged in Eurasia, distinct conceptions of the construct reflect their geopolitical interests. Russia’s conception of ‘Sphere of Influence’ and resisting Western dominance in its backyard is one of its main geopolitical objectives in Eurasia. For China, the region is important for both economic and security interests. For the US and the West, Eurasia is seen as a theatre for containing Russia and China, the heartland’s dominant powers. While all such distinct national conceptions of Eurasia treat Central Asia as the locus region, the term itself has become a ‘definitional morass’, evading strict definitions or geographical strictures.

For India, Eurasia is not merely geographical but a civilizational and strategic continuum rooted in ancient linkages spanning across millennia. Much before the Silk Road, the Indian subcontinent, or South Asia today, frequently exchanged ideas, commodities, peoples and philosophies with this region. In the twenty-first century, it represents India's extended neighbourhood beyond the maritime domain, encompassing energy-rich Central Asia, the Caspian Sea linked-Caucasus region, and Russia. Afghanistan also occupies a pivotal place in India’s conception of Eurasia as it serves as an interface between Central and South Asia, and is sometimes treated simultaneously as part of India’s immediate and extended neighbourhoods.

Unlike the Western view of Eurasia as a heartland prize or Russian civilizational narrative, India's conception of Eurasia emphasises mutual respect for sovereignty, multipolarity, and balanced partnerships. The region itself is vital for India's energy security - oil, gas, uranium and critical minerals. The forces of extremism and radicalisation in the region, especially in the Afghanistan-Pakistan border region, makes the area of strategic interest to India. As a result, India has promoted counter-terrorism cooperation with Afghanistan and the Central Asian republic. Another major driving force in India’s Eurasia calculus include the imperative of trade diversification with this underexplored region, and to prevent its encirclement by any single power.

New Delhi's potential focus on the Eurasian region is also driven by its historical and cultural ties to Eurasian countries, especially Russia and the Central Asian Republics. For India’s Eurasia strategy, Central Asia serves as the core, Afghanistan as a gateway, the South Caucasus as a strategic partner for shared interests in regional connectivity, and Russia as a reliable partner. India rejects zero-sum games and aspires to forge strategic partnerships and alliances with countries with common interests in regional stability, economic development, and multilateral cooperation. India's view avoids ideological framing, focusing on developmental partnerships and is rooted in the principle of strategic autonomy.

New Delhi continues to describe the region as part of its ‘extended neighbourhood’ and a ‘natural partner.’ Yet, this narrative has not translated into tangible strategic or economic gains. The Eurasian region presents immense economic opportunities for India. By leveraging its historical connections with the region, India aims to foster stronger people-to-people relations, promote tourism, and enhance cultural diplomacy. Rich in natural resources and strategically located along key trade routes, the region offers the potential for enhanced trade, investment, and energy cooperation.

India can tap into these markets, diversify its economic engagements, and strengthen its energy security. India's engagement with Eurasia is also crucial for maintaining a balance of power in the region as it seeks to promote a multipolar Eurasian order as a precursor to a just multipolar world. Unlike China and Russia's increasing assertiveness in Eurasia through initiatives such as the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) and the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO), India however, lacks strong institutional grounding or a regional grouping of its own through which it can actively participate in safeguarding its interests and counterbalance regional imbalances.

In the contemporary era, India's foreign policy has leaned towards the maritime domain (Indo-Pacific, Act East, Quad). On closer enquiry, this is partly due to the colonial legacy of the partition of South Asia in 1947 and the subsequent Pakistani refusal to allow India passage to Afghanistan and Central Asia. These structural constraints have led to relative Indian neglect of continental Eurasia in the last seven decades, despite enduring civilizational ties and several material linkages predating the partition of the subcontinent. India’s ‘Connect Central Asia’ policy in 2012 marked a shift, but implementation lagged amid maritime priorities and continuing instability in Afghanistan.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s visit to all the five Central Asian countries in 2015 signalled a high point in India’s regional outreach. However, high-level exchanges have since remained limited; the last state visit to India by a Central Asian leader was of Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev in 2018. Even though India-Central Asia relations matured in the last decade, beginning with the institutionalisation of dialogue at the foreign ministers’ level in 2019, the first India–Central Asia Summit convened virtually in 2022, and the SCO Summit under India’s presidency held in a virtual format in 2023, the absence of sustained, in-person high-level engagements has contributed to a perception that India’s engagement with Central Asia has lost momentum.

Broader geopolitical developments, including the fallout of the Russian-Ukrainian war, tensions in West Asia centring Iran, and shifting Eurasian connectivity dynamics, are reshaping the strategic calculations of the regional countries in Eurasia. Regional states are increasingly pursuing multi-vector foreign policies while expanding their engagement with a wide range of external partners. These developments, while presenting a complex geopolitical situation, are opening a sliver of opportunity for India. The country is well-placed as a neutral balancer with strong and resilient ties with Russia and Central Asian countries.

However, limited connectivity and the gap between policy formulation and implementation continue to hinder India’s Eurasia strategy. To bridge this gap, India must adopt a consolidated, multi-pronged continental strategy prioritising alternative connectivity; including exploring air and digital connectivity. Leveraging soft power, including expanding educational cooperation, promoting cultural connections, bolstering people-to-people contacts and capacity-building programmes must be given high priority. In the absence of direct connectivity, incentivised investments (especially by private sector and through global arms of Indian public sector undertakings), localisation of bilateral economic activities, and digital cooperation have huge potential to grow.

Integrating Eurasia into India's broader grand strategy by balancing its maritime and continental dimensions is essential for sustained, meaningful engagement in the region. Despite geopolitical, logistical, and infrastructural barriers, New Delhi can steadily expand its influence through consensual partnerships that prioritize mutual respect for sovereignty and shared prosperity. Reclaiming India’s continental thinking in terms of foreign and defence policy does not necessarily mean undermining its maritime priorities. It only needs a thorough, interest-based reassessment of India’s strategic alignments through a bold engagement with the region and an ability to think beyond the obvious.

Against this evolving backdrop, the India Eurasia Research Forum (IERF) stands uniquely positioned to bridge persistent gaps and accelerate sustained, high-impact engagement between India and Eurasian stakeholders. As a dedicated platform focused exclusively on India-Eurasia ties, unlike broader think tanks with diversified mandates, IERF delivers targeted, high-quality research and facilitates multi-stakeholder dialogues. It convenes Track 1.5 and Track 2 initiatives that bring together government officials, domain experts, civil society, academia, and private-sector actors to address priority domains. This will include Physical and digital connectivity (including INSTC optimization, Chabahar synergies, air/digital corridors, and emerging tech linkages), security and counter-terrorism cooperation, energy security and critical minerals, cultural and people-to-people ties (education, tourism, capacity-building, and heritage diplomacy) and multipolarity and balanced regional dynamics.

Through regular seminars, webinars, policy roundtables, and Track 1.5 exchanges, IERF will generate actionable outputs such as commentaries, policy briefs, articles, joint research publications, and facilitate bilateral/multilateral exchanges. These efforts amplify India's strategic voice in Eurasian discourse while ensuring reciprocal insights flow back to New Delhi. This will help foster mutual understanding and consensus-driven partnerships.

In a rapidly transforming Eurasia, marked by multi-vector foreign policies and connectivity realignments, IERF will serve as a vital enabler. By driving evidence-based continental re-engagement, it will help India build enduring strategic depth that complements its continental priorities, safeguarding national interests through sovereignty-respecting cooperation and shared prosperity.
publications.authorBio: Dr. Pravesh Kumar Gupta is an Associate Fellow at the Vivekananda International Foundation (VIF). He is also the Research Advisor to the India Eurasia Research Forum (IERF). Dr. Gupta is an expert on Eurasian geopolitics and his research focuses on the society and politics of Central Asia, energy security and sustainability, and trans-regional connectivity linkages between Central and South Asia.

guidelines: Structured & Correct: Articles should be well-written and factually correct.
Original Content: Submissions must not have been published elsewhere.
No in-text citations: IERF does not use endnotes or in-text citations.
Hyperlinks only: All references must be hyperlinked directly in the text.
Pitching: We accept unsolicited submissions, but pitching first is welcome.
